findings.headline: £172k deficit on borrowing and investment costs against revised budget
findings.detail: Net result on borrowing costs and investment income was £172k worse than revised budget. Higher Q4 borrowing rates and HRA capital timing effects drove the variance.
findings.matters: Confirms actual interest cost pressures exceeded forecast even in revised budget
findings.figures: £172k net deficit
findings.quote: Investment and borrowing interest for 202 5/26 have produced a net deficit of £172k against the revised budget

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing from councils peaked at 7% in late Q4 2025-26
findings.detail: Rates for LA market borrowing rose from 4-4.5% to peaks of 7% in February and March 2026, driven by base rate uncertainty and geopolitical tensions. The council's £74.5m of short-term debt captured these elevated rates.
findings.matters: High short-term rates increase current debt service and refinancing risk; exposes council to roll-over costs when rates are expensive
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing £74.500m at 5.10% average rate (ranges 4-7% during year)
findings.quote: from late 2025 rates began to rise, peaking at around 7% in February and March 2026

findings.headline: LOBO loan repaid after lender exercised option to raise rate from 3.95% to 7%
findings.detail: Bayerische Landesbank invoked its lenders option in May 2025 to increase the rate on the council's final LOBO loan by 403 basis points. The council repaid the loan in full rather than accept the increase and replaced it with short-term market borrowing.
findings.matters: Demonstrates exposure to embedded rate risk in LOBO structures; shows how lender options can force unplanned refinancing into expensive markets
findings.figures: LOBO rate struck at 7% from 3.95%
findings.quote: In May 20 25, the one remaining LOBO loan (Lenders Option, Borrowers Option) the Council had with Bayerische Landesbank, was repaid in full as the lender exercised their right to increase the loan rate from 3.95% to 7%

findings.headline: £38.5m PWLB debt for commercial property investments cannot be refinanced
findings.detail: The council holds £38.5m of PWLB debt from prior commercial property purchases. The revised CIPFA Prudential Code now restricts PWLB from financing investment property, so this debt cannot access PWLB replacement funding when it matures.
findings.matters: Creates refinancing risk on material debt; maturity of these loans could force asset sales or force borrowing from higher-cost sources
findings.figures: £38.500m PWLB debt for commercial investments
findings.quote: The Council currently holds PWLB debt of £ 38.500m for commercial investments that were purchased prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code

findings.headline: Unable to access PWLB; forced to borrow from LA market at higher rates
findings.detail: PWLB rates were significantly elevated due to rising gilt yields and fiscal concerns. The council sourced all £13.02m of new borrowing from the local authority market instead, indicating it cannot access its traditional primary borrowing source at acceptable cost.
findings.matters: LA market borrowing is more expensive and volatile than PWLB; signals reduced access to stable, long-term financing
findings.figures: £13.020m new borrowing entirely from LA market
findings.quote: All new borrowing undertaken in 2025/26 was temporarily from the LA market, since PWLB rates were much higher

findings.headline: Net borrowing increased by £12.48m to £199.2m in a single year
findings.detail: The council's net borrowing position (after accounting for reserves) grew from £186.72m to £199.2m, a 6.7% increase. This reflects both capital expenditure needs and reduced available reserves for internal borrowing.
findings.matters: Growing leverage constrains future borrowing capacity and increases debt service obligations that must be funded from revenue
findings.figures: £12.480m increase; net borrowing £199.200m (was £186.720m)
findings.quote: the Authority had net borrowing of £ 199.200 arising from its revenue and capital expenditure, an increase on 2025/26 of £12.480m

findings.headline: Property and Assets service experienced £110k utility cost overspend across operational assets.
findings.detail: The Property & Assets service reported a £83,845 total overspend (1.45% of revised budget). Of this, £110k relates to utility costs across the Council's operational assets that exceeded budget. This was partially offset by £120k savings from Minster Exchange opening and other minor service underspends.
findings.matters: Rising utility costs signal emerging operational pressure on facilities management that may recur; if structural, this represents cost inflation that could affect future budget sustainability.
findings.figures: £110,000 utility cost overspend; £83,845 total service overspend; £5,788,571 revised budget; £120,000 partial offset from Minster Exchange
findings.quote: This variance is primarily due to an overspend of £110,000 utility costs across the Council's operational assets, together with overspends on property management staffing costs andf legal costs associated with the planned sale of assets.

findings.headline: From 2026/27, council faces £425k new annual cost to fund county rough sleeping services, previously funded separately by government.
findings.detail: Cheltenham received homelessness grant funding of £1,016k in 2025/26 (including a £76k windfall). However, from 2026/27 onwards, the council will be required to contribute up to £425k annually to county-wide rough sleeping services directly from its homelessness prevention grant, whereas these costs were previously met from separate government funding. The council is setting aside approximately £220k from 2025/26 grant balances in preparation.
findings.matters: This represents a new recurring £425k annual obligation that will compress the council's homelessness budget and require either additional funding sources or reallocation from other priorities; it is a material structural change to the council's ongoing cost base.
findings.figures: £425k annual contribution required from 2026/27; £1,016k total homelessness grant 2025/26; £220k being set aside; £405k grant increase 2025/26 with anticipated formula changes for 2026/27
findings.quote: from 26/27 Cheltenham will be required to make a direct contribution to the provision of county-wide rough sleeping services from its homelessness prevention grant of up to around £425k, whereas for 2025/26 and in previous years these costs were met from a separate pot of grant funding

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - General Fund Capital Programme Outturn 2025-26 & Revised Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Delivery scheme shows zero spending in 2025-26 against a £4.5m allocation
findings.detail: CAP227 Housing Delivery, budgeted at £4.5m for 2025-26 to enable Private Rented Sector delivery in partnership with registered social landlords, recorded no expenditure in the outturn (shown as "-"), with the full £4.5m continuing to be budgeted in all subsequent years through 2028-29.
findings.matters: Failure to deploy allocated capital on a strategic housing delivery commitment raises questions about the council's project execution capability and whether announced strategic initiatives can be reliably delivered.
findings.quote: Enabling the delivery of Private Rented Sector (PRS) Housing. 4,500,000 - 4,500,000 4,500,000 4,500,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - General Fund Capital Programme Outturn 2025-26 & Revised Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: National Cyber Innovation Centre represents a £68m capital commitment by 2027-28 with interest costs rising to £2.3m annually
findings.detail: The council's capital programme shows the Cyber Innovation Centre at Golden Valley escalating from a £28.6m budget in 2025-26 (with only £430k spent) to £68m by 2027-28, funded through borrowing. Interest costs on this borrowing climb from £440,000 in 2026-27 to £2,322,000 in 2027-28.
findings.matters: This multi-year borrowing commitment will materially increase the council's debt service costs and constrain future financial flexibility. Lenders need clear visibility of the scale and trajectory of this strategic debt.
findings.quote: Interest costs for Delivery of the National Cyber Innovation Centre at Golden Valley. 440,000 2,322,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - General Fund Capital Programme Outturn 2025-26 & Revised Programme 2026-27
findings.headline: Delta Place Renovations spent £3.5m against a budget of £31,550 — an 11,200% overspend
findings.detail: A capital project originally budgeted at £31,550 resulted in actual spending of £3,538,226. This represents either a fundamentally failed cost estimate, uncontrolled scope creep, or a project that failed to trigger escalation controls when costs spiralled.
findings.matters: Cost overruns of this magnitude reveal critical weaknesses in project governance and cost control that directly affect lender confidence in the council's financial management.
findings.figures: Budget £31,550; Outturn £3,538,226
findings.quote: CAP527 Delta Place Renovations 31,550 3,538,226 3,538,226

findings.paper_title: General Fund Housing Revenue Account - Outturn Report 2025-26 - report
findings.headline: Council's own risk assessment flags high probability of being unable to close the medium-term financial strategy funding gap without unplanned service cuts
findings.detail: Risk 52 in the council's risk register is assessed as high-risk (Impact 5/5, Likelihood 4/5) and states the council will struggle to prepare budgets without cuts if unable to close the MTFS gap. This indicates the council does not currently have a sustainable long-term financial plan and its own finance leadership is uncertain about structural sustainability.
findings.matters: This signals a structural problem beyond the current budget cycle. The council's own finance leadership is flagging that sustainable year-on-year budgeting without service cuts is at significant risk, which threatens financial stability and debt service capacity beyond the medium term.
findings.figures: Risk 52 rated at Impact 5/5, Likelihood 4/5, raw score 20/25
findings.quote: If the Council is unable to come up with long term solutions which close the gap in the medium term financial strategy then it will find it increasingly difficult to prepare budgets year on year without making unplanned cuts in service provision.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Housing Revenue Account - Outturn Report 2025-26 - report
findings.headline: Business rates revaluation and significant rate changes in 2026/27 will create material income volatility during a period when the budget is already tight
findings.detail: The council states it expects business rates to 'remain an area of significant challenge going forwards' due to revaluation and rate changes by the Valuation Office. Additionally, business rates collection declined in 2025/26 (from 97.64% to 97.19%), indicating underlying economic stress. This income uncertainty is likely to coincide with the period when the council depends on unidentified savings.
findings.matters: Business rates income is inherently volatile during revaluation cycles, particularly in weak economic conditions. This compounds the risk of undelivered savings, creating potential for a double-impact income and savings gap in 2026/27.
findings.figures: Business rates collection fell to 97.19% in 2025/26 from 97.64% in prior year; revaluation and rate changes scheduled for 2026/27
findings.quote: In 2026/27 there has been a rest of business rate values by the Valuation Office and significant changes in the rates being applied to local businesses so we expect this to remain an area of significant challenge going forwards.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Housing Revenue Account - Outturn Report 2025-26 - report
findings.headline: The council's financial plan for 2026/27 is dependent on delivering £1.054m in savings, with no identified source for these savings
findings.detail: The report states the reserve recovery plan 'assumes during 2026/27 delivery of savings totalling £1.054m as well as cover off any emerging financial pressures during the year in full.' This is an explicit and critical assumption but the savings appear not yet identified. If not delivered, the council cannot use reserves (already below optimum) without further depletion, leaving unplanned service cuts as the only option.
findings.matters: An undelivered savings plan means automatic deficit and forced service cuts. Given the council has balanced recent years through revenue underspends rather than identified savings, this creates material risk that 2026/27 will face a funding gap with no flexibility to address it.
findings.figures: £1.054m savings target for 2026/27; council's recent history of relying on year-end underspends rather than planned savings
findings.quote: It should be noted that assumes during 2026/27 delivery of savings totalling £1.054m as well as cover off any emerging financial pressures during the year in full.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Housing Revenue Account - Outturn Report 2025-26 - report
findings.headline: General Fund balance of £1.459m is below the Section 151 Officer's assessed optimum level of £1.5m, following two consecutive years of reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council used £646k of reserves in 2025/26 despite a £16k revenue underspend. The report explicitly notes that '2024/25 and 2025/26 have seen a need to continue to rely on usage of general fund balances.' This pattern of drawdown is unsustainable and leaves the council with inadequate financial flexibility for unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves below the assessed minimum level limit the council's ability to manage unexpected costs or income shortfalls without unplanned service reductions. A lender assesses financial resilience based on reserve adequacy and trend.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £1.459m vs assessed optimum of £1.5m; reserve usage of £646k in 2025/26; pattern continuing from prior year
findings.quote: This leaves the General Fund balance at £1.459m with a plan to add just below £316k during 2026/27 to bring these reserves to an optimum level.

findings.headline: Savings targets identified for 2026-27 general fund and HRA are flagged as a governance focus area
findings.detail: The council has identified savings across both general fund and HRA budgets for 2026-27 and listed delivery of these savings as a key governance issue requiring active management in the coming year.
findings.matters: Identified savings that do not materialise are a major red flag for lenders; flagging this as a governance risk suggests delivery uncertainty, particularly given the constrained finance function.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: To deliver the savings identified in the 2026/27 general fund and HRA budgets

findings.headline: External auditors have raised issues on 2024-25 accounts that require council response
findings.detail: The council identifies a need to effectively respond to issues raised by external auditors in relation to 2024-25 accounts and the ongoing 2025-26 audit. The specific nature of these issues is not detailed in this statement.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit findings indicate control deficiencies; the ability to respond depends on adequate finance team capacity, which was previously constrained.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: we are able to effectively respond to the issues raised by our external auditors in relation to the 2024/25 accounts and during the audit of 2025/26 accounts

findings.headline: Finance team capacity pressures caused delays in financial processes during 2025-26
findings.detail: Cheltenham experienced significant capacity pressures within the finance team during 2025-26, contributing to delays in financial processes. Although additional capacity has been added, the council explicitly flags that this must be monitored during 2026-27 to ensure accounts are published on time and external audit issues can be properly addressed.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity is fundamental to the control environment and timely financial reporting; delays in accounts preparation affect audit clearance and stakeholder confidence in financial controls.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: During 2025/26 we experienced significant capacity pressures within the finance team, which contributed to delays in our financial processes. Whilst additional capacity has now been added it will be essential that this is monitored during 2026/27 to ensure that our accounts are published on time

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Only 50% of 2025/26 audit actions have been implemented to date, with five Priority 1 (major concern) actions still open.
findings.detail: Of 14 actions agreed following 2025/26 audits, only 7 have been actioned. More concerning, the council has 5 Priority 1 actions outstanding—these are defined as areas of major concern requiring immediate corrective action. This slow implementation rate for high-priority findings creates ongoing risk exposure.
findings.matters: A 50% implementation rate on agreed audit actions, particularly when Priority 1 actions remain open, suggests audit recommendations are not being treated with appropriate urgency. This affects the reliability of financial reporting and management controls.
findings.figures: 7 of 14 actions implemented (50%); 5 Priority 1 actions outstanding; Priority 1 defined as 'areas of major concern requiring immediate corrective action'
findings.quote: Of the 14 actions agreed in 2025/26, 7 have been actioned. We rank our actions on a scale of 1 to 3, with 3 being medium or administrative concerns to 1 being areas of major concern requiring immediate corrective action.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Two audit actions from 2024/25 remain outstanding past their implementation date, indicating slow remediation of known control issues.
findings.detail: Internal audit notes that two agreed actions from the prior year audit cycle have not been completed despite passing their scheduled implementation dates. This pattern of overdue remediation suggests either insufficient management capacity or prioritisation issues in addressing known control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Delayed remediation of audit findings indicates either weak management of agreed improvements or competing priorities that prevent control remediation. For a lender, this raises questions about management commitment to addressing identified risks.
findings.figures: 2 historic (2024/25) actions outstanding past implementation date
findings.quote: There are currently two historic (2024/25) outstanding agreed action which have passed their implementation dates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Assurance opinion is Reasonable, not Substantial, indicating control weaknesses exist.
findings.detail: Internal audit gave Cheltenham a Reasonable Assurance opinion for 2025/26, which means some issues and scope for improvement were identified that may put at risk the achievement of objectives. This is lower than Substantial, where controls operate effectively. Five audits did achieve Substantial Assurance, but the overall opinion reflects identified gaps.
findings.matters: A lower assurance level signals governance or control gaps that could affect financial reporting, service delivery, or risk management. Lenders assess this as an indicator of management oversight and internal control strength.
findings.figures: Reasonable Assurance given (not Substantial); 5 Substantial, 1 Reasonable, 0 Limited opinions in 2025/26
findings.quote: On the balance of our 2025/26 audit work for Cheltenham Borough Council, enhanced by the work of external agencies, I am able to offer a Reasonable Assurance opinion in respect of the areas reviewed during the year.

findings.headline: HRA capital expenditure significantly underran forecast, reducing expected borrowing requirement
findings.detail: Capital expenditure against the Housing Revenue Account came in well below estimate, which in turn reduced the debt that needed to be recharged to HRA for the year.
findings.matters: Suggests difficulty executing capital programme as planned; may indicate delivery delays, slippage, or constraints on capital spending that could affect asset maintenance or development.
findings.figures: No specific amount disclosed, only noted as 'well below estimated spend'
findings.quote: The HRA capital expenditure was well below estimated spend and this resulted in less debt recharged to the HRA for 2025/26.

findings.headline: Treasury management produced a £172k net deficit against revised budget, driven by borrowing costs exceeding forecast by £224k
findings.detail: While a small variance in absolute terms, the £172k deficit was driven by borrowing costs running £224k over budget, offset partially by investment income outperforming by £52k. The council attributes the borrowing variance to 'higher rates available towards the back end of the financial year added with additional borrowing to cover the daily cashflow.'
findings.matters: Treasury costs are rising faster than budgeted; higher rates and increased operational borrowing for cashflow management are combining to pressure finance costs.
findings.figures: Net treasury deficit £172k; borrowing cost variance £224,447 over budget; investment income surplus £52,074
findings.quote: The reason for the variance is mainly due to the higher rates available towards the back end of the financial year added with additional borrowing to cover the daily cashflow.

findings.headline: Last LOBO loan repaid in May 2025 after lender exercised option to increase rate from 3.95% to 7%
findings.detail: The council's final LOBO loan with Bayerische Landesbank was forced to repayment when the lender exercised its contractual right to increase the rate by over 3 percentage points. The council replaced this with short-term debt after seeking external advice.
findings.matters: Demonstrates exposure to lender-initiated rate shocks beyond council control; LOBO structures proved hostile; replacement with short-term debt exacerbated refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Rate increase from 3.95% to 7.00% (3.05 percentage point shock)
findings.quote: In May 2025, the one remaining LOBO loan (Lenders Option, Borrowers Option) the Council had with Bayerische Landesbank, was repaid in full as the lender exercised their right to increase the loan rate from 3.95% to 7%. It was decided to repay the loan after seeking advice from Arlingclose and replaced the loan with short term debt.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing surged by £21.450m while long-term fell by £8.430m; LA market rates peaked at 7% in Feb-Mar 2026
findings.detail: The council's borrowing composition shifted markedly, with short-term borrowing rising from £53.050m to £74.500m while long-term fell from £151.359m to £142.930m. All new borrowing in 2025-26 came from the LA market because PWLB rates were 'very expensive' due to higher gilt rates. Crucially, LA rates spiked from their normal 4-4.5% to around 7% in February and March 2026.
findings.matters: This creates substantial refinancing risk: 38% of total debt (£82.500m) matures within 12 months and will need to be rolled over at potentially much higher rates than historically available.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing increased £21.450m to £74.500m; long-term fell £8.430m to £142.930m; LA market rates peaked at 7% in Feb-Mar 2026; 38% of debt due within 12 months
findings.quote: All new borrowing undertaken in 2025/26 was temporarily from the LA market, since PWLB rates were much higher as they were affected by higher gilt rates... from late 2025 rates began to rise, peaking at around 7% in February and March 2026.

findings.headline: Schroder pooled fund underperforming by £116k with oil and gas exposure despite ESG commitments
findings.detail: The Schroder Income Maximiser Fund currently stands at £116k less than the original £2m invested. The fund contains £59k (0.84%) in oil and gas investments. The council has committed to divesting from oil and gas "in the longer term" but is balancing this with financial prudence, suggesting the fund may not be sold at an advantageous price.
findings.matters: The fund's underperformance and continued exposure to assets the council wants to divest from indicate investment selection risk and potential for further losses if divestment occurs at disadvantageous prices.
findings.figures: £2m invested, current value £116k less (5.8% loss); oil/gas exposure £59k (0.84% of £7m pooled funds)
findings.quote: However, the current capital value of the fund is valued £116k less than the original £2m invested. Given our current climate priorities, assurance was provided to Council that we are looking to take steps to ensure our investments are contributing to these goals. We are committed in the longer term to divesting from oil and gas but need to balance these priorities with ensuring we are making the right financial decisions.

findings.headline: Strategy relies on internal resources to defer external borrowing, with over-borrowing reaching £185m by 2028
findings.detail: Internal over-borrowing (using reserves rather than external loans) will grow from £36.469m (31.3.26) to £100.658m (31.3.27) to £185.404m (31.3.28). The council is deliberately using short-term borrowing and internal cash while long-term rates remain elevated, but this creates a timing risk: eventually internal resources will be exhausted and the council must access external markets.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess when the council will need to refinance these internal borrowings and at what rates; if interest rates rise before the council accesses external markets, debt service costs will be higher than planned.
findings.quote: As demonstrated by the liability benchmark in table 1, the Council expects to be a long-term borrower and new treasury investments will therefore be made primarily to manage day-to-day cash flows using short-term low risk instruments.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement will expand by 60% over four years, requiring up to £60m in new borrowing
findings.detail: The CFR has grown from £215.8m (31.3.25) to £240.969m (31.3.26) and is forecast to reach £305.158m by March 2027 and £389.904m by March 2028. The expansion is driven by the HRA's affordable housing capital programme and the General Fund Cyber Innovation project. The council will need to access borrowing markets significantly to fund this expansion.
findings.matters: The scale of borrowing needed materially affects the council's debt service costs and refinancing risk, particularly if the council needs to borrow at rates higher than currently forecast.
findings.figures: CFR 31.3.27 £305.158m, CFR 31.3.28 £389.904m (vs 31.3.25 actual £215.840m); £60m new borrowing required over forecast period
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme especially within the HRA capital programme to deliver on our affordable housing target, but also on the General Fund in regard to the Cyber Innovation project. With minimal investments the council will therefore be required to borrow up to £60m over the forecast period.

findings.headline: Property investments of £62.3m are financed substantially by £39.2m of borrowing; investment security depends on market valuations staying above original purchase cost.
findings.detail: The council's £92.6m total investment portfolio is dominated by property assets (£62.3m), with 43% financed by borrowing (£39.2m). The council's model for assessing investment security depends on fair value remaining at or above purchase cost including transaction costs, while acknowledging property values fluctuate.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess concentration risk: if property markets decline, both investment returns fall and the asset security supporting £39m of borrowing could be questioned, potentially requiring financial restructuring.
findings.figures: Commercial investments property £62,297,000 (book value 31.03.2025); financed by borrowing £39,169,000 (2026-27 forecast)
findings.quote: In accordance with government guidance, the Authority considers a property investment to be secure if its accounting valuation is at or higher than its purchase cost including taxes and transaction costs. It is understood that the fair value of property will fluctuate.

findings.headline: Council's operating budget depends on achieving 12% of expenditure from investment income, with explicit risk of reserve depletion if targets are missed.
findings.detail: Service expenditure of £45.763m requires £5.601m of investment income. The strategy document explicitly states that if investment targets are not achieved, the authority will need to draw from reserves or generate emergency savings to continue providing services.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council's operating budget can survive if investment returns fall short; this also represents a potential pressure on reserves if market performance is poor.
findings.figures: Service expenditure £45,763k, Investment income £5,601k (2026-27 forecast), representing 12.24% of budget
findings.quote: Should it fail to achieve the expected income targets, the Authority will be required to draw additional balances from reserves or generate savings elsewhere within the budget to continue to provide its services.

findings.headline: Housing stock brought in-house in 2023; HRA now accounts for 50% of capital programme
findings.detail: The council took housing services back into-house in 2023 and is now committing £43.328m to HRA improvements in 2026/27, including £25m in internal improvements (kitchens, bathrooms, rewiring), £4.4m in fire protection works, and £7.1m in external and communal upgrades. This is a major operational and financial commitment.
findings.matters: In-house housing operations add complexity and operational risk. The scale of the internal improvement programme suggests legacy maintenance backlogs. Fire protection at £4.4m indicates potential compliance gaps that now need funding.
findings.figures: HRA capital: £43.328m; internal improvements £25m; fire protection £4.4m; external/communal upgrades £7.1m
findings.quote: Significant internal improvements, including kitchens, bathrooms and rewiring, ensure our homes meet modern quality and safety standards. £25m... Fire protection works, including enhanced systems in communal areas, ensure regulatory compliance and resident safety. £4.4m

findings.headline: Interest rates on new borrowing at 4–6% in tightening rate environment
findings.detail: The council cites current rates of approximately 4% for short-term borrowing and 5.5–6.0% for long-term fixed-rate loans. Financing costs are currently 4.64% of net revenue spend in 2026/27, but this ratio is trending upward as debt grows faster than revenue.
findings.matters: With £305m+ of outstanding debt by 2027, even small moves in interest rates can materially impact the revenue budget. The council's interest rate risk exposure is rising as it takes on more debt.
findings.figures: Short-term loans ~4%; long-term fixed rates 5.5–6.0%; financing costs 4.64% of revenue in 2026/27 (up from 4.32% in 2025/26)
findings.quote: The Council's main objectives when borrowing are to achieve as low and certain cost of finance as is available at the time of need while retaining flexibility should plans change in future... short-term loans (currently available at around 4%) and long-term fixed rate loans where the future cost is known but higher (currently 5.5% to 6.0%).

findings.headline: Capital receipts acknowledged as finite resource; proactive asset disposal programme required to manage borrowing
findings.detail: The council recognises that capital receipts from asset sales are limited and has committed to 'a proactive drive to identify a pipeline of sites to consider for disposal' to reduce reliance on borrowing. The Asset Management Strategy is under review to identify surplus or underutilised property.
findings.matters: This dependency on asset sales to manage the debt trajectory means the council's financial position is exposed to property market conditions and execution risk on disposals. Failed sales directly impact debt repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Capital receipts forecasted at £9.434m in 2026/27 (GF £5.494m + HRA £3.940m)
findings.quote: Capital receipts from the disposal of assets represent a finite funding source and it is important that a planned and structured manner of disposals is created to support our priorities... To reduce the Council's reliance on borrowing there is a proactive drive to identify a pipeline of sites to consider for disposal.

findings.headline: Maintenance now funded by borrowing rather than reserves; council plans to sell strategic sites to manage debt
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states that 'a large amount of planned maintenance work is currently proposed to be funded by borrowing which will increase the pressure on the revenue budget', and notes that 'the sale of some strategic sites would provide capital to replace this borrowing'. This represents a shift from the historical funding model and creates execution risk on asset disposals.
findings.matters: Funding routine maintenance through debt rather than reserves signals budget stress and creates dependency on asset sales. If property sales do not materialise as planned, revenue pressure will rise sharply.
findings.figures: HRA capital programme £43.328m in 2026/27; significant portion of this dependent on future asset sales
findings.quote: A large amount of planned maintenance work is currently proposed to be funded by borrowing which will increase the pressure on the revenue budget. The sale of some strategic sites would provide capital to replace this borrowing

findings.headline: Golden Valley development and National Cyber Innovation Centre represents £101.7m single investment
findings.detail: This is by far the largest single capital commitment in the programme, described as strengthening Cheltenham's position as a national centre for cyber innovation. The investment is positioned as core to the council's economic recovery strategy and long-term prosperity.
findings.matters: A loan book lender needs to assess whether this single bet on economic recovery and cyber sector growth is likely to generate the returns needed to service the debt, and what happens if the cyber sector stalls or the development underperforms.
findings.figures: £101.7m for Golden Valley development including National Cyber Innovation Centre
findings.quote: Investment in the Golden Valley development, including delivery of the National Cyber Innovation Centre and associated financing costs, strengthens Cheltenham's position as a national centre for cyber innovation and high value employment. £101.7m

findings.headline: Capital expenditure and borrowing more than double year-on-year
findings.detail: The council's planned capital spending jumps from £40.293m in 2025/26 to £85.655m in 2026/27. Debt financing for this programme is £47.776m, up from £22.572m the previous year. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is forecast to increase by £64.19m in 2026/27 alone, with total outstanding debt projected to reach £305.158m by March 2027.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this debt trajectory is sustainable and whether the revenue budget can support the rising interest costs.
findings.figures: £85.655m capital expenditure 2026/27; £47.776m debt financing; £64.19m CFR increase; £305.158m total CFR by 31.03.2027
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the Council is planning capital expenditure of £85.655m as summarised below... The CFR for our Council is expected to increase by £64.19m during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Reserve position reverses from building in 2025/26 to drawing in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council contributes to reserves in 2025/26 (£487,526 to Business Rates Reserve, £415,881 to earmarked reserves) but then draws from them in 2026/27 (£558,541 from Business Rates Reserve, £123,671 from earmarked reserves). This marks a material shift from reserve accumulation to reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns reduce financial resilience and typically indicate tightening budget position; a shift from building to depleting reserves is a material deterioration in financial trajectory.
findings.figures: Business Rates Reserve: +£487,526 (2025/26) to -£558,541 (2026/27); Earmarked reserves: +£415,881 to -£123,671
findings.quote: Contribution to/(from) Business Rates Retention Reserve 487,526 (558,541) Net contribution to/(from) earmarked reserves 415,881 (123,671)

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision jumps by over £900,000 in 2026/27, indicating increased debt servicing
findings.detail: MRP swings from a credit of (£9,396) in 2025/26 to a charge of £905,317 in 2026/27, then stabilises at £90,000 per annum from 2027/28 onwards. This discontinuity suggests either new borrowing is being incurred in 2026/27 or a change in the council's debt portfolio that creates materially higher debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: A lender requires visibility on debt profile changes; this level of swing raises questions about what's driving the new borrowing and whether it's sustainable given the reported savings delivery problems.
findings.figures: MRP/VRP: (£9,396) → £905,317 → £90,000+ per annum ongoing
findings.quote: Minimum Revenue Provision & VRP (9,396) 905,317 90,000 90,000

findings.headline: Savings planned for 2025/26 were not delivered, adding pressure to subsequent years
findings.detail: The MTFP explicitly notes 'unrealised savings from 2025/26'. The savings strategy shows a £1,024,259 target in 2025/26 that becomes (£1,053,750) negative in 2026/27, indicating not only did planned savings fail to materialise but the deficit position worsened. This suggests either the council's savings plans were over-optimistic or operational barriers prevented delivery.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that planned savings will be delivered; failed savings undermine the credibility of future MTFP projections and increase risk of future budget gaps.
findings.figures: Savings strategy: £1,024,259 (2025/26) to (£1,053,750) (2026/27); Net Cost of Services grows from £17,978,126 to £20,796,899 over the plan period

findings.headline: Autumn 2024 increase in Employers National Insurance (to 15.8%) is unfunded in the 2026/27 settlement despite housing staff being directly employed by the council since July 2024
findings.detail: The government increased Employers National Insurance contributions from 13.8% to 15.8% from April 2025, but provided no funding to cover the HRA's share of the increase for directly employed housing staff who transferred to the council in July 2024.
findings.matters: An unbudgeted cost pressure means modelled HRA finances do not match actual running costs, creating a gap that must be closed elsewhere
findings.figures: Employer NI increase from 13.8% to 15.8%; threshold reduced from £9,100 to £5,000; housing staff brought in-house July 2024
findings.quote: The Final Local Government Finance Settlement for 2026/27 does not include funding for the increase in the contributions for housing staff whose salaries are covered by the HRA, despite being directly employed by the Council since July 2024

findings.headline: Void rate at 2.7% against 2.0% target due to capacity constraints in turning around empty properties
findings.detail: The council is unable to re-let empty homes fast enough. Current void rate of 2.7% is above the 2.0% target 'caused by issues in capacity to turn around void properties'. Officers are reviewing capacity to reduce the turnaround time.
findings.matters: Each percentage point of voids directly reduces rental income; at 2.7% the council is losing roughly 0.7% of potential rental income below target
findings.figures: Void rate 2.7% actual vs 2.0% target; rental income from dwellings £25m budgeted
findings.quote: The void rate is currently 2.7% against a target of 2.0% caused by issues in capacity to turn around void properties

findings.headline: Capital programme will increase HRA borrowing by £23.478m, with interest modelled at 3.52% and identified as a significant long-term risk to sustainability
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme is expected to add £23.478m to HRA debt. Interest payable is modelled at an average rate of 3.52% for 2026/27 (falling to 3.25% in future years). The council's 30-year business plan 'identifies interest cover as a significant risk factor in the long term affordability of the operation of the HRA'.
findings.matters: High debt service costs relative to revenue reduce operational flexibility and expose the council to further interest rate rises
findings.figures: £23.478m new borrowing planned 2026/27; 3.52% average rate; £350k interest savings assumed in medium term
findings.quote: the programme is expected to increase levels of borrowing by £23.478m which places a significant pressure on the HRA operational budget as interest rates remain high

findings.headline: £1.300m cladding safety programme is contingent on government funding; if the Cladding Safety Scheme is rejected, HRA must find additional savings beyond the planned £650k
findings.detail: Three blocks (Arle Road, Grevil Road, Orchard Way) have combustible external cladding assessed as 'unacceptable level of risk' in January 2025. The council is applying to government for full funding. The s151 Officer has stated in writing that without this external funding, 'additional savings over and above the already identified £650k...would need to be found', putting sustainability at risk.
findings.matters: A material unfunded liability that could force service cuts or debt if the government scheme does not pay out, affecting both HRA stability and borrowing headroom
findings.figures: £1.300m budget for cladding removal; three 5-storey blocks identified; fire risk assessment January 2025
findings.quote: Without external funding the risk to ensuring financial sustainability remains a risk and therefore additional savings over and above the already identified £650k in cluded within the HRA operational budget would need to be found if external funding is not agreed

findings.headline: HRA reserves fell below the £1.5m minimum target for the first time in 2023/24 and are recovering only slowly
findings.detail: The council is implementing a recovery plan centred on £650k savings from the housing service transition and £350k from interest reduction by 2027/28. However, the Cladding Safety Scheme decision will determine whether reserves can actually build. The council notes reserves remain 'around the bare minimum levels they should be even with external funding'.
findings.matters: A council whose reserves are below safe minimums has no buffer for unexpected costs and signals stress to lenders
findings.figures: £1.5m target, fell below it for first time 2023/24, £1m total savings planned over 2026/27-2027/28
findings.quote: the HRA balance which fell below the target of £1.5m for the first time in 2023/24

findings.headline: Capital financing strategy depends on asset disposals whose timings 'are currently under review'
findings.detail: The council states that 'the delivery of capital receipts from asset management activities is an important source of funding' for a £41.4m capital programme spanning 2025/26 to 2028/29. However, delays to asset disposals are explicitly named as a driver of current-year overspend, and the paper notes that timings are 'currently under review.' This creates uncertainty around capital delivery and liquidity.
findings.matters: If asset sales slip, the council will need to borrow or cut capital schemes. Delays are already happening. A lender needs clarity on which capital schemes are essential and which can be deferred.
findings.figures: £41.420m capital programme for 2025/26; timings under review
findings.quote: The delivery of capital receipts from our asset management activities is an important source of funding with the timings and delivery of these currently under review... The key drivers of this position are non-delivery of savings and delays to asset disposals.

findings.headline: General Fund Balances are being drawn down in the current year despite planned contribution, requiring rebuild
findings.detail: The council planned to add £0.560m to General Fund Balances in 2025/26 but instead is forecasting a drawdown of £0.101m, reducing balances from £1.286m to £1.184m. To rebuild to the minimum required level of £1.5m, the 2026/27 budget includes a contribution of £0.316m. At £1.5m, this represents 7.5% of a £20m net budget—a thin buffer for a council facing 18.6% funding cuts and undelivered savings.
findings.matters: Reserves cushion unexpected events. A council in structural deficit and drawing down balances while facing large funding cuts has limited financial flexibility. The minimum level of 7.5% is modest for current financial uncertainty.
findings.figures: Current year drawdown: £0.101m; balances fall to £1.184m; 2026/27 contribution £0.316m; minimum set at £1.5m (7.5% of budget)
findings.quote: Following a detailed review of all budgets, savings, and asset disposals, the latest forecast is an overspend of £0.662m. This means that instead of contributing to General Fund Balances as planned, there will be a drawdown of £0.101m, reducing the balance from £1.286m to £1.184m by the end of 2025/26... In order bring the level of General Fund Balances up the required level of £1.5m the 2026/27 budget proposal include a contribution £0.316m.

findings.headline: A significant business rates revaluation appeal has created a £1.016m deficit that depletes the stabilisation reserve
findings.detail: The council's statutory NNDR1 form shows a £1.016m share of the business rates collection fund deficit, 'largely due to a significant revaluation appeal during the year.' Accounting rules require this to impact 2026/27. The council holds a Business Rates Retention Equalisation Reserve to absorb such shocks, but has had to increase it to £500k specifically to accommodate this hit.
findings.matters: Business rate volatility is creating calls on reserves. A single appeal has consumed the stabilisation capacity for one year. In a council already drawing down balances and facing large funding cuts, this limits flexibility.
findings.figures: £1.016m business rates deficit; Equalisation Reserve increased to £500k
findings.quote: There is also an issue in the current year relating to business rates, following completion of the statutory NNDR1 form at the end of January 2026. This is largely due to a significant revaluation appeal during the year. The Council's share of the deficit on the Business Rates Collection Fund is £1.016m, and accounting rules require that this impacts the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.headline: Revenue funding to fall by 18.6% over three years with no named solution to emerging budget gaps
findings.detail: Cheltenham's government funding drops from £7.698m in 2025/26 to £6.270m in 2028/29. Revenue Support Grant alone falls from £4.353m to £3.279m (a 25% cut). The council has identified budget gaps of £0.491m in 2027/28 and £0.666m in 2028/29, which it describes as 'projections that will continue to be refined' but offers no named savings plans to close them.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council will close £1.16m of forecast gaps over two years when it is already struggling to deliver savings in the current year. Council tax increases are capped at 2.99% and cannot be relied upon to fill such a large gap.
findings.quote: The settlement is relying upon increases in council tax to make up the shortfall... The forecast of service costs and expected resources is set out in Appendix 16. The projected budget gaps for each year are: 2027/28: £0.491m; 2028/29: £0.666m.

findings.headline: Savings programme failed to land in 2025/26, driving an overspend that will be repeated in current year forecasts
findings.detail: The council forecast a 2025/26 overspend of £0.662m, explicitly attributing this to 'non-delivery of savings and delays to asset disposals.' For 2026/27, a new £1.054m savings target has been set, delivered through staffing, base budget, discretionary service and capital reviews. However, monitoring will not begin until Q1, and the paper does not state that prior-year savings are now on track.
findings.matters: A council that has not delivered savings targets in the current year and relies on undelivered savings to balance next year's budget presents execution risk. This is a pattern to watch.
findings.figures: £0.662m current year overspend; £1.054m savings target for 2026/27
findings.quote: Following a detailed review of all budgets, savings, and asset disposals, the latest forecast is an overspend of £0.662m. This means that instead of contributing to General Fund Balances as planned, there will be a drawdown of £0.101m... The key drivers of this position are the non-delivery of savings and delays to asset disposals.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation in April 2028 will transfer all council assets and liabilities to a new unitary authority, requiring £1m in implementation costs.
findings.detail: The council will cease to exist in April 2028 under the Gloucestershire unitary proposal. The budget reflects this by allocating £1m to the New Initiatives Reserve 'in recognition of the LGR implementation costs', and the council is explicitly planning staffing and budget alignment for the transition.
findings.matters: LGR creates 18 months of operational uncertainty and diverts resources away from service delivery; the finite lifespan constrains long-term borrowing and capital planning decisions.
findings.figures: £1m allocated to New Initiatives Reserve for LGR costs; reorganisation date April 2028
findings.quote: Part of the process has been to top up... the New Initiatives Reserve to £1m in recognition of the LGR implementation costs. Local Government Reorganisation in two-tier areas, which is scheduled to be implemented by April 2028, would mean that the Council would cease to exist, with its assets and liabilities being transferred to a new unitary council.

findings.headline: The Finance Team has experienced loss of key personnel and corporate knowledge, addressed through interim support.
findings.detail: The report notes 'There has been a loss of key personnel and corporate knowledge' in the Finance Team, mitigated by interim support. This is a governance and operational risk that affects the council's capacity to manage financial control.
findings.matters: Finance team turnover and reliance on interim staff can compromise budget control, forecasting accuracy, and the reliability of financial management during a period of structural pressure.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: There has been a loss of key personnel and corporate knowledge. This has been addressed through the use of interim support.

findings.headline: Government funding is forecast to fall £1.428m over three years, with a £0.492m budget gap emerging in 2027/28.
findings.detail: Fair Funding allocations decline from £7.698m (2025/26) to £7.218m, £6.762m, and £6.270m across the three-year settlement. The S151 officer forecasts a £0.492m budget gap in 2027/28, requiring further savings or service reductions.
findings.matters: Structural, predictable funding decline limits the council's financial flexibility and signals ongoing austerity despite the Fair Funding Review.
findings.quote: Over the medium term, Cheltenham's Fair Funding allocations from government are forecast to fall from £7.698m in 2025/26 to £7.218m in 2026/27, £6.762m in 2027/28, and £6.270m in 2028/29. The forecast budget gap for 2027/28 is estimated to be £0.492m.

findings.headline: Non-delivery of savings was the key driver of the 2025/26 overspend; the council now targets £1.054m in new savings for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The S151 officer explicitly identifies 'non-delivery of savings' as a key item causing the current year's £0.662m overspend. The 2026/27 budget requires £1.054m in savings through staffing reviews, base budget efficiency, discretionary service review, and capital project review.
findings.matters: Repeated failure to deliver savings is a red flag for budget reliability and governance; future savings targets rest on the same planning process that has just failed.
findings.figures: £1.054m savings target for 2026/27; prior year non-delivery contributed to £0.662m overspend
findings.quote: The key items driving this position are non-delivery of savings and delays to asset disposals... The resulting savings target for 2026/27 is £1.054m

findings.headline: Cheltenham is drawing on reserves in 2025/26 instead of building them, due to a £0.662m overspend.
findings.detail: The council forecasts a £0.662m overspend for 2025/26, reversing the planned £0.560m contribution to General Fund Balances into a £0.101m draw. This reduces balances from £1.286m to £1.184m—a material depletion of the council's buffer.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown during an overspend signals financial stress and reduces the council's ability to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: £0.662m overspend; £0.101m draw on reserves; balances fall from £1.286m to £1.184m
findings.quote: Following a detailed review of all of budgets, savings and asset disposals the latest forecast is an overspend of £0.662m for year. This means that instead of contributing to General Fund Balances there will be draw on them of £0.101m

news_drafts.headline: £172k deficit on borrowing and investment costs against revised budget
news_drafts.lead: Confirms actual interest cost pressures exceeded forecast even in revised budget

news_drafts.headline: Short-term borrowing from councils peaked at 7% in late Q4 2025-26
news_drafts.lead: High short-term rates increase current debt service and refinancing risk; exposes council to roll-over costs when rates are expensive

news_drafts.headline: LOBO loan repaid after lender exercised option to raise rate from 3.95% to 7%
news_drafts.lead: Demonstrates exposure to embedded rate risk in LOBO structures; shows how lender options can force unplanned refinancing into expensive markets
